title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 209: The Deep-Ocean Mining Frontier
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 209 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Deep-Ocean Mining Frontier

Paragraph 1. Four thousand metres beneath the Pacific Ocean lies the Clarion-Clipperton Zone (CCZ), a pitch-black plain stretching five million square kilometres between Hawaii and Mexico. Covering the muddy seabed are trillions of potato-sized mineral lumps called polymetallic nodules. These rocks hold more nickel, cobalt, copper, and manganese than all land mines combined—essential materials needed to manufacture batteries for electric vehicles.

Paragraph 2. Mining companies argue that gathering loose seabed nodules causes less harm than digging mines on land. Company director Gerard Barron points out that land mining in several countries causes severe deforestation, child labour, and toxic waste runoff, whereas the deep seabed has no forests to clear or local villages to move. Marine biologists strongly reject this view. Surveys reveal that more than eighty percent of animals found in the CCZ are brand new to science. Because freezing 1°C water and scarce food force creatures to grow slowly, ecosystems recover poorly. Furthermore, glass sponges and giant single-celled creatures depend strictly on hard nodule surfaces as their only solid anchor.

Paragraph 3. Long-term experiments confirm how fragile deep benthic life is. In 1989, German scientists scraped a three-kilometre seabed strip off the coast of Peru to imitate mining machines. When an international team revisited the site in 2019—thirty years later—the scraped tracks still looked fresh, and sessile animal numbers remained eighty-five percent lower than in untouched areas. Beyond seabed scars, giant mining crawlers will pump mud and nodules up to surface ships, then discharge millions of gallons of leftover slurry back into midwater. Ecologist Dr. Diva Amon warns these drifting mud clouds could suffocate jellyfish and carry toxic metals into commercial tuna and swordfish fisheries.

Paragraph 4. Legally, international seabed minerals are managed by the International Seabed Authority (ISA), headquartered in Kingston, Jamaica. While some island states hope mining contracts will bring income, a coalition of over twenty-five nations—including France and Germany—demands an immediate pause until deep-sea risks are fully understood. Meanwhile, scientists insist the real answer lies in cobalt-free battery designs and mandatory electronics recycling worldwide.

q1.text: Electric car factories already buy half of their nickel from the Pacific Ocean floor.

steps: Đoạn 1: Chỉ nêu trữ lượng khoáng sản dưới đáy biển rất lớn để làm pin xe điện, không nói các hãng xe đã mua một nửa từ đáy biển.

q2.text: Most animals collected in the Clarion-Clipperton Zone were already well known to science.

steps: Đoạn 2: Hơn 80% loài thu thập được hoàn toàn mới với khoa học (brand new to science).

q3.text: Certain deep-sea sponges need the hard surfaces of mineral nodules as a place to attach.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...glass sponges... depend strictly on hard nodule surfaces as their only solid anchor."

q4.text: Thirty years after the 1989 Peru test, seabed animal populations had returned completely to normal.

steps: Đoạn 3: Sau 30 năm số lượng sinh vật bám vẫn thấp hơn 85% so với vùng chưa bị xáo trộn.

q5.text: More than twenty-five countries want to pause ocean mining until risks are clearly understood.

steps: Đoạn 4: "...over twenty-five nations... demands an immediate pause until deep-sea risks are fully understood."
Đoạn 3: "...discharge millions of gallons of leftover slurry..."
